cases.name: FCC v. Brown
cases.summary: The Fourth Circuit’s mandamus order requiring the Federal Communications Commission to resolve an application for review within 48 hours of its entry is stayed because the order improperly interferes with the Commission’s discretion to determine the timing and procedures of its deliberative process.
cases.lineup_text: PER CURIAM. On March 30, 2026, the Media Bureau of the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) issued a “public notice” about the FCC’s lowest unit charge (LUC) requirements. Those requirements, which are outlined in 47 U. S. C. §315(b)(1)(A), concern favorable rates that broadcasters must charge for campaign advertisements in the weeks leading up to elections. The notice stated that political candidates, joint fundraising committees with noncandidate members, and political parties engaged in coordinated political activity are entitled to the LUC. Four candidates for Congress filed an application for review with the FCC, arguing that only political candidates are entitled to the LUC and asking the full Commission to set aside the public notice as unlawful. Two months later, while their application was still pending before the Commission, the candidates filed a petition for review against Per Curiam the FCC and the United States in the Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit seeking the same relief. cases.name: Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church
cases.summary: The Government is entitled to a stay of the preliminary injunction halting border-barrier construction because it is exceedingly likely to establish that the District Court lacked jurisdiction under §102(c)(2)(A) of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 over respondents’ claim that the Secretary of Homeland Security’s waiver of statutory requirements violated the major-questions doctrine.
cases.lineup_text: PER CURIAM. Section 102 of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA) grants the Secretary of Homeland Security broad authority to construct border barriers and roads “to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” §102(a), 110 Stat. 3009–554, as amended, note following 8 U. S. C. §1103. The same section expressly authorizes the Secretary “ ‘to waive all legal requirements’ ” as “ ‘necessary to ensure expeditious construction’ ” of those barriers and roads, §102(c)(1), 119 Stat. 306, and sharply limits judicial review of all claims arising from such waiver determinations. Specifically, the statute provides that “ ‘[a] cause of action or claim may only be brought alleging a violation of the Constitution of the United States’ ” and courts “ ‘shall not have jurisdiction’ ” over nonconstitutional claims. §102(c)(2)(A).
